observations.quote: it is requisite that wee treat here a little more largly of the Syderyall or invisible man, to wit, of his Originall and power
observations.note: The author announces a fuller treatment of one subject, set apart from what goes before: the Syderyall or invisible man, his Originall and power.

observations.quote: If Aristotle had taken notice of this Olympick Spirit, and Galen made more account of it, there had not such errors crept into Philosophy and Physick springing from the heathenish masters of errors
observations.note: The author holds that errors crept into philosophy and physick because Aristotle and Galen did not regard the Olympick Spirit; he calls these sources heathenish masters of errors and sets aside, for now, what they did to divinity.

observations.quote: The invisible man or Olimpick Spirit is borne in us after this manner.
observations.note: The invisible man and the Olimpick Spirit are given as two names of one thing, and the account of its birth in us is announced.

observations.quote: were taken (as hath been sayd) ex LIMO TERRAE
observations.note: The words 'as hath been sayd' point back to an earlier place where Adam and Eve's being taken from the earth was said; the lines given do not show which.

observations.quote: ex LIMO TERRAE, out of the dust of the ground or great world
observations.note: The Latin words are Englished in the text itself as the dust of the ground, and the ground is equated with the great world; the mortal body taken from it is said to be both visible and invisible.

observations.quote: For the whole frame of the world is collected and reduced into the Microcosm, so that there is nothing to be found in all the world but the same also is in one man.
observations.note: The whole world is gathered into the Microcosm; whatever is in the world is also in one man.

observations.quote: The Physicall, Elementary, visible and Tangible body is from the Earth: but the Invisible, Insensible, Sydereall body (which is the house or cottage of the Spirits life) is from the Astra's of the Firmament
observations.note: Two bodies with two origins: the visible from the Earth, the Sydereall from the Astra's of the Firmament. The Sydereall body is called the house or cottage of the spirit's life.

observations.quote: Thus Adam had two bodies, that is, a visible Elementall, and an invisible Sydereall body.
observations.note: Adam is said to have had two bodies, named as a pair: a visible Elementall and an invisible Sydereall body.

observations.quote: an incorporeall Astralick man which moveth, guideth, and performeth all skilfull matters
observations.note: At every birth two men are born: the visible man is called the organ and instrument of the invisible; the Astralick man moves, guides and performs all skilful things.

observations.quote: an incorporeall Astralick man
observations.note: The invisible man is here called incorporeall, while the same paragraph calls it a body ('an invisible Sydereall body') and the margin note N122 says not only visible things are bodies. Recorded as wording that does not sit evenly; no judgement.

observations.quote: For the Astra's now in Man doe by Man alwayes in generation produce those two
observations.note: The Astra's that are in man produce both bodies in generation, through man.

observations.quote: The visible Elementary body of flesh and blood in the mothers womb out of the four Elements
observations.note: The visible body is made in the womb out of the four Elements.

observations.quote: the invisible Sydereall body that is capable of attaining Phylosophy is from the Astra's of the Firmament
observations.note: The Sydereall body, not the elementary one, is said to be the one capable of attaining philosophy.

observations.quote: For that little world Man is one and the same in all things with his-Parant, the great world
observations.note: Man is called the little world and the great world his parent; the two are said to be the same in all things.

observations.quote: But as the great world is distinguished by its shell or out-side from the Angelicall world, so man the little world is distinguished by his skin or out-side from the great world.
observations.note: Three worlds are set apart each by an outside: the great world by its shell from the Angelicall world, man by his skin from the great world.

observations.quote: That which is sensible and that which is insensible hath a sydereall spirit or a sydereall body in it.
observations.note: The margin extends the sydereall spirit or body to all things, sensible and insensible; spirit and body are given as alternative names.

observations.quote: Eve is Adam transplanted. The first men were created, the rest proceed from the Being of the seed or Esence.
observations.note: The margin calls Eve Adam transplanted and sets the created first men against the rest, who proceed from the seed, equated with Esence.

observations.quote: The Spirit of life is the Spiracle or breathing hole.
observations.note: The margin says what the Spirit of life is: the Spiracle, Englished as breathing hole.

observations.quote: The body of the Limbus & spiracle ought to make one Marriage
observations.note: The body of the Limbus and the spiracle should be joined as in one marriage; the words that follow, on adultery and bastardly blood if not, are partly illegible.

observations.quote: For as in all thing the marriage or joynting together of two is the perfection
observations.note: The joining of two is given as the perfection in all things; the rest of the sentence has illegible letters.

observations.quote: it is a body because bodies are the fruits thereof and without a body such fruit cannot grow
observations.name: Paracelsus
observations.note: The margin reports what Paracelsus 'saith' (the first letters of the name are illegible; a writing of his is pointed to with vide) of the element of fire: it is a body, since bodies are its fruits. The words before this quote are partly illegible.

observations.quote: So the wind is a body and like a visible body hath power to overturne another body
observations.note: The wind is given as a body that is not seen. The note does not show whether this still reports Paracelsus or is the author's own.

observations.quote: Not onely visible things are bodies, for God created as well visible as invisible bodies of the same power.
observations.note: Bodies are said to be of two kinds, visible and invisible, of the same power. Whose words these are is not shown in the note.

observations.quote: The inner Man ascendeth the inward Heaven.
observations.note: An inner Man and an inward Heaven are paired.

observations.quote: This Spirit is tha Doctor of true Astronomy.
observations.note: The spirit discussed is called the teacher of true Astronomy.

observations.quote: (Gabalis Homo) coagulated or curdled Man
observations.note: The Latin name is Englished in the text itself as coagulated or curdled Man; it stands in a row of names (Sydereall, Internall, Olimpick, Incorporeall) for the man said to be the same with the Firmament of the Astra's.

observations.quote: as hath been often said
observations.note: Points back to earlier places saying this inner man is the same with the Firmament; the lines given do not show which.

observations.quote: is the same with the Firmament of the Astra's, as hath been often said, like rednesse with wine, whitenesse with snow, or the lustre of the Sun with the Aire
observations.note: The sydereall man is said to be one with the Firmament of the Astra's; three likenesses show the manner: as a quality is one with the thing that has it.

observations.quote: this sydereall body is called the Genius of man, because it proceedeth from the Firmament
observations.note: Genius is given as a name of the sydereall body, with its reason: it comes from the Firmament.

observations.quote: it is called Penates, because it is in our power and born with us
observations.note: A second name with its reason: Penates, because it is in our power and born with us; it is also called the shadow of the visible body.

observations.quote: Lar domesticus the good or bad houshould or private Angell
observations.note: A further name, Englished in the text as the good or bad household or private Angel.

observations.quote: the Umbratile or shadowy Man
observations.note: A further name, Englished as shadowy.

observations.quote: the familiar Homuncle (or little Man) of the Sophies (or wise men,)
observations.note: Homuncle is Englished as little Man and Sophies as wise men; the name is given as the one the Sophies use.

observations.quote: Paracelsus his internall Adech
observations.name: Paracelsus
observations.note: Adech is given as Paracelsus' own name for the same thing.

observations.quote: that which first inwardly formeth in our mind what we afterward outwardly fashion with our hands
observations.note: The text says what Adech means (i. e.): what first forms inwardly in the mind what the hands afterwards fashion outwardly.

observations.quote: the Spectrum, ghost, or fantasie, the Light of Nature
observations.what: the Spectrum, ghost, or fantasie, the Light of Nature
observations.note: Further names in the same row, all for the sydereall body; Light of Nature is one of them.

observations.quote: the presaging or Propheticall Euestrum that foretelleth any thing by signes
observations.note: A further name with what it does: the Euestrum foretells by signs, in man.

observations.quote: It is also called ahe imagination, which incloseth all the Astra's, and is indeed all the Astra's or Starrs
observations.note: The same thing is also called the imagination; it is said to contain all the Astra's, to be all of them, and to hold the same course, nature and power with heaven.

observations.quote: by which I do not meane the seaven visible coales of Heaven which are but the bodyes of the Astra's but I meane the invisible and insensible body of all things or Astrall Spirit
observations.note: Stated: the author says his word Astra's or Stars is not meant of the seven visible lights of heaven, which are only their bodies, but of the invisible body of all things or Astrall Spirit.

observations.quote: they are nothing else but the verue or powers of the Angells
observations.note: The Astra's are further said to be nothing but the powers of the Angels.

observations.quote: The Angells which live only upon the vision of God, are the created wisdome of God
observations.note: The text says what the Angels are: the created wisdom of God.

observations.quote: he that knowes God, he knows the Astra's also: He that knowes the Astra's cannot but knowe the world, and consequently man the off-spring of the world
observations.note: A chain of knowing: from God to the Astra's, to the world, to man, called the offspring of the world.

observations.quote: The Astra's form & bring forth all bodily things out of themselves, and multiply themselves together with those bodily things that are brought forth
observations.note: The Astra's make all bodily things out of themselves and multiply along with them.

observations.quote: the seeds of any graine or Wheat is the Astrum, viz. the invisible body, which being cast into the Earth it produceth a visible body
observations.note: The text's own example of an Astrum: the seed of a grain, called the invisible body, which sown brings forth a visible body and many more Astra's.

observations.quote: the Astrum is nothing else but the insensible, invisible body, or living Spirit, yet without Reason in things that grow; but with reason in living things, as in man
observations.note: The Astrum is defined as the invisible body or living Spirit: without Reason in growing things, with reason in living things such as man.

observations.quote: Bodyes are nothing else but the Excrement of the Astra's
observations.note: Bodies are said to be nothing but the Excrement of the Astra's, brought forth into bodily being by their operation.

observations.quote: This every Astrum can doe of it selfe, as by imagination to bring forth of it selfe another Astrum in a body
observations.note: Each Astrum brings forth another Astrum in a body, by imagination, forming it by operation.

observations.quote: There is no body without an Astrum
observations.note: Every body has an Astrum; the sentence goes on past the note mark with the converse.

observations.quote: as there is no Astrum without a visible body.
observations.note: The converse: no Astrum is without a visible body.

observations.quote: The eating of the apple produceth this body the sydereall seed into force & vigour.
observations.note: The margin ties the sydereall seed's coming into force to the eating of the apple.

observations.quote: Astrum, Vulcanus and Archaeus are the same thing, & but one Spirit yet without Reason, & divers, as are the divers formes of severall things.
observations.note: Three names, Astrum, Vulcanus and Archaeus, are made one Spirit, without Reason, and differing as the forms of things differ.

observations.quote: but one Spirit yet without Reason
observations.note: The margin calls the Astrum a spirit without Reason with no limit; MICRO.32 says the Astrum is without Reason in growing things but with reason in living things, as in man.

observations.quote: The Astralick Spirit is every growing thing standeth in need of a corporeall habitation.
observations.note: The Astralick Spirit is said to need a bodily dwelling; the note stands beside the sentence that no body is without an Astrum.

observations.quote: The inner Man is Heaven it selfe or all the Astras.
observations.note: The inner Man is equated with Heaven itself, or all the Astras.

observations.quote: Read in Picus how Trimethius put upon himselfe the various Evestra's of the three-fold world one after another, & transformed himselfe into several shapes
observations.name: Picus
observations.note: The margin sends the reader to Picus for an account of Trimethius putting on the Evestra's of the three-fold world and changing his shape.

observations.quote: by reall Magick he shewed to that great Picus the hidden virtue or power of Man
observations.note: Man's power, who was created after the image of God, is called hidden; it was shown to Picus by real Magick.

observations.quote: We are transformed into that which we most intently gaze and meditate upon.
observations.note: A rule: we become what we most intently look at and think on.

observations.quote: The understanding of Man is assimulated to all things.
observations.note: Man's understanding is said to be made like all things.

observations.quote: The impression of the Imagination from fear, terrour, & griefe
observations.note: The note ties sickness and death to what fear, terror and grief impress on the Imagination; one letter of the word that follows is illegible.

observations.quote: The Astra's send the plague into us through our skin as the Sun doth his beams thhrough the glasse.
observations.note: The Astra's send the plague through the skin, as sunbeams pass through glass.

observations.quote: whereas the imagination of Man is not one, but all the Astra's, it is as true that it produceth not onely one, but many operations
observations.note: Because man's imagination is all the Astra's, it produces many operations, not one.

observations.quote: the Gate of Wonders, the spring and originall of all Magicall operations, and hath power to beget and bring forth visible bodies without detriment or diminution of the Astrall and sydereall Spirit
observations.note: The imagination, though incorporeall and invisible, is called the Gate of Wonders and the source of all magical operations, able to bring forth visible bodies without loss to the Astrall Spirit. Just before the quote the text reads 'being joyned to a heightned the Gate of Wonders'; the lines given do not show what it is joined to.

observations.quote: and can work any wonderfull operations whatsoever, present or absent, above the reach of humane Reason.
observations.note: Its operations are said to work at hand or at a distance, and beyond human reason.

observations.quote: The Light of Nature makes bodily things visible, but Eternall things are to be seen onely by Faith
observations.note: Two ways of seeing: the Light of Nature for bodily things, Faith for eternal things.

observations.quote: The child in the mothers womb is strangely marked by the impression of the imagination without any bodily touch
observations.note: The marking of the unborn child is given as an instance of imagination working without bodily touch.

observations.quote: What we doe visiby by the body, that doe we by Faith after the manner of Spirits
observations.note: What the body does visibly, Faith does in the manner of Spirits.

observations.quote: Thus the Imagination breedeth the Plague and such like Firmamentall diseases; it brings sicknesse and health.
observations.note: The Imagination is said to breed the Plague and like diseases, called Firmamentall, and to bring both sickness and health.

observations.quote: the Sydereall and Animall Spirit (which is the mechanick Astrall Spirit)
observations.note: The Sydereall and Animall Spirit, also called the Spirit of the lesser world, is glossed as the mechanick Astrall Spirit.

observations.quote: The Pestilence which comes by fear, trouble and terrour, riseth by the imagination of the Spirit of the lesser world
observations.note: The pestilence that comes by fear rises from the imagination of the sydereall and animall spirit in man.

observations.quote: as we see in women with childe who give marks and tokens to the young in their womb by the same sydereall Spirit
observations.note: The same spirit is said to be what marks the child in the womb.

observations.quote: This sydereall Spirit which is born of the Astra's together with Man (and therefore remains united to the Astra's) is the Load stone and hath a magnetick nature in man.
observations.note: The sydereall Spirit is called the Load stone in man, with a magnetic nature; it stays united to the Astra's because it is born of them.

observations.quote: so also the body and spirit in Man doe draw unto him by a visible body, this is the Load stone of the Microcosm
observations.note: Set beside the earthly Load stone: body and spirit in man draw to him; this is named the Load stone of the Microcosm.

observations.quote: The sydereall body and spirit attract unto them the force of the Astra's, as we see in those that are Lunatick
observations.note: The sydereall body and spirit draw the force of the Astra's; the Lunatick are given as the instance.

observations.quote: This fourth kind of Naturall Magick called Gamahaea doth all things invisibly and spiritually, by the help of Art
observations.what: fourth kind of Naturall Magick called Gamahaea
observations.note: A named, numbered kind of Natural Magick: the fourth, called Gamahaea. It does invisibly by Art what Nature does visibly without it.

observations.quote: This fourth kind of Naturall Magick
observations.note: Calling this the fourth kind points to other kinds named elsewhere in the writing; the lines given do not show them.

observations.quote: The House is as it were dead, but the Inhabitant to wit, the Spirit of perpetuall motion of invisible Nature or the magnetick spark of the Soule of the world liveth and worketh effectually
observations.note: A figure flagged by 'as it were'. Stated: the Inhabitant is said ('to wit') to be the Spirit of perpetual motion of invisible Nature or the magnetick spark of the Soule of the world. The House is not explained in this sentence.

observations.quote: workmanship, Arts, Sciences, and the knowledge of all things lie hid in the Astra's of the Firmament
observations.note: All wisdom, arts, sciences and knowledge are said to lie hidden in the Astra's of the Firmament; the sentence begins before the note mark with 'All Animall wisdome'.

observations.quote: There is nothing so hidden in the world which is not praefigured in the Astra's
observations.note: Whatever is hidden in the world is said to be prefigured in the Astra's.

observations.quote: all the Astra's of the Firmament, which are the Tincture of the speculation of our mind
observations.note: The Astra's of the Firmament are called the Tincture of the speculation of our mind.

observations.quote: can of their own in-bred or naturall force by imagining produce bodily and visible things out of that which doth not appear
observations.note: The Astra's by imagining bring visible things out of what does not appear; a great cloud rising in a clear sky is the instance.

observations.quote: which though they were Nothing before production, yet being produced out of invisible things, they become great bodies.
observations.note: Rain, snow, hail and the like are said to have been Nothing before, and to become great bodies out of invisible things.

observations.quote: all things in the first Creation were produced out of the DIVINE NOTHING, or invisible Cabalisticall Poynt, into something
observations.note: From the cloud the author draws the first Creation: all things out of the DIVINE NOTHING, also named the invisible Cabalisticall Poynt, done by God in a moment.

observations.quote: All things proceeded out of the invisible Darknesse, and were called out to the visible Light by the WORD speaking, and the Spirit cherishing.
observations.note: All things came from invisible Darkness to visible Light by the WORD speaking and the Spirit cherishing.

observations.quote: the whole Imagination of Man dependeth on the Astra's of the Firmament, yea is the same and abideth one with them
observations.note: Man's Imagination is said to depend on the Astra's of the Firmament and to be one with them, as his Sydereall body is from them.

observations.quote: it must needs be that the Firmament also hath an Imagination but without Reason, as Man the off-spring of the world hath with Reason
observations.note: The author concludes that the Firmament too has an Imagination, without Reason, as man has one with Reason.

observations.quote: One man striketh and hurteth another, and that with Reason, a nettle and fire burne and hurt without Reason.
observations.note: The instance given for hurting with Reason and without it.

observations.quote: the Astra's do those things which Humane wisdom desireth
observations.note: The Astra's do what human wisdom desires; the words before it link Wisdome with Inchantment and have an illegible letter.

observations.quote: In respect of the Elementatary body it is a Spirit and performeth all spirituall operations.
observations.note: Set against the elementary body, it is a Spirit and does all spiritual operations; the note does not name what 'it' is.

observations.quote: all actions and events of Men are pictured in the Astra's, every living Creature hath its Ascendant signe in Heaven
observations.note: Heaven is said to know all things; men's actions and events are pictured in the Astra's and every living creature has its Ascendant sign.

observations.quote: Every Body is proceeded of an invisible & incomprehensible subsisting Spirit.
observations.note: Every body comes from an invisible Spirit.

observations.quote: is a three fold NIHIL or Nothing, a Divine, Privative and Negative NOTHING
observations.note: Three kinds of NIHIL or Nothing are named: Divine, Privative and Negative. The word that is said to be this is illegible.

observations.quote: The whole Heaven is nothing else but the Imagination
observations.note: The whole Heaven is said to be nothing but the Imagination; the note stands beside the paragraph that says the Firmament has an Imagination.

observations.quote: It breedeth the Plague and and Fevers in
observations.note: It is said to breed the Plague and Fevers; the words that follow have an illegible letter.

observations.quote: whereas Man is the Quintessence of the greater world, it follows that Man may not onely imitate Heaven, but rule it also at his beck
observations.note: Man is called the Quintessence of the greater world; from this the author draws that man may rule Heaven, not only imitate it.

observations.quote: All things naturally obey the Soule, and must of necessity move and work toward that which the soule earnestly desireth
observations.note: All things are said to obey the Soul and work toward what it earnestly desires, when it is carried with vehement desire.

observations.quote: when by holinesse we draw vertue from him who is the true Archetype, and when we ascend to him, then every Creature must and will obey us
observations.note: The condition is stated: the powers of the world serve us when by holiness we draw virtue from him who is called the true Archetype and ascend to him.

observations.quote: By the help of Imagination all Magicall operations and all wonderfull things are done through the Naturall inborn Faith
observations.note: All magical operations are done by Imagination through the Naturall inborn Faith, by which we are at peace with the Spirits.

observations.quote: so the incorporeall cogitation of Man worketh on the subject, by the spirit onely as with a visible instrument
observations.note: The Imagination is said to work in man like the Sun: as the bodily Sun burns without an instrument, man's thought works on a thing by the spirit alone, as if with a visible instrument.

observations.quote: what the visible body doth that also doth the invisible body
observations.note: The invisible body does whatever the visible body does; after the note mark the instance is the sydereall man doing hurt to another.

observations.quote: The Imagination of Man is the Loadstone that attracteth above a 1000 miles off
observations.note: The Imagination of man is called the Loadstone that draws from far off; in its Exaltation it draws what it will out of the Elements.

observations.quote: unles first it attract the thing conceived by the attractive force of the imagination, that it may beget the Architect of the Imagination as a native spirit out of it selfe
observations.note: First step named as needed for the Imagination to work: it draws in the thing conceived and so begets the Architect of the Imagination, a spirit out of itself.

observations.quote: afterward the Imagination being as it were with child maketh impression, which though it be not tangible, yet it is corporeall like the wind
observations.note: Second step, in a figure flagged by 'as it were': the Imagination, as if with child, makes an impression, said to be not tangible yet corporeall like the wind.

observations.quote: By Faith we may do good or evillus God permitteth.
observations.note: By Faith good or evil may be done, as God permits.

observations.quote: the true Magician or wise Man can attract the operation of the Astra's, stones, mettalls, &c. into the Imagination
observations.note: The true Magician, also called wise Man, can draw the operation of the Astra's, stones and metals into the Imagination, as a burning glass brings the Sun's beams and heat to us.

observations.quote: The Imagination can produce whatever we see with our eyes in the greater world
observations.note: The Imagination is said to be able to produce whatever is seen in the greater world.

observations.quote: Thus by Imagination and true Gabalia all hearbs, all growing things, all mettalls may be produced.
observations.note: Herbs, growing things and metals may all be produced by Imagination and true Gabalia.

observations.quote: This part of Magick is called Gabalisticall, and is supported with three Pillars.
observations.what: This part of Magick is called Gabalisticall
observations.note: Names one part of Magick and announces three Pillars, which the next three paragraphs number.

observations.quote: Magick or Faith transplanting minds hath power over all Spirits and Ascendants.
observations.note: Magick and Faith transplanting minds are set side by side as one thing, with power over all Spirits and Ascendants.

observations.quote: First, with TRUE PRAYERS made in Spirit and Truth
observations.note: The first Pillar of Gabalisticall Magick, numbered and set in capitals.

observations.quote: when God is prayed unto in the internall Spirit, not with noyse of words, but in a sacred silence, without opening the mouth and groaning
observations.note: How the prayer is made: inwardly, in silence, without words or opening the mouth.

observations.quote: Secondly, by NATURALL FAITH, or in-born Wisdome
observations.note: The second Pillar, numbered and set in capitals; also called in-born Wisdome, given by God equally to all men in the Creation.

observations.quote: Thirdly, by a strongly exalted IMAGINATION
observations.note: The third Pillar, numbered and set in capitals; its strength is said to be shown by the Light of Nature.

observations.quote: as well in Jacobs Rods mentioned by Moses
observations.name: Moses
observations.note: Jacob's Rods, as Moses mentions them, are given as an instance of imagination's force; the margin note N129 gives the place.

observations.name: Gen.
observations.note: The note names the writing and place beside the mention of Jacob's Rods.

observations.quote: as in pregnant women who imprint the mark of that which they long for upon the child, as hath been said
observations.note: The words 'as hath been said' point back within this writing; in the lines given the marking of the child stands at MICRO.33 and MICRO.34.

observations.quote: The Imagination or Fantasie of Man is like the Load stone in its Nature, attracting the Fantasie of other men, as we see in those that gape and yawn.
observations.note: Imagination, also called Fantasie, draws the Fantasie of other men as the Load stone draws; yawning is the instance.

observations.quote: A vehement Imagination doth not onely cause a transmutation of ones own body, but sometimes also of anothers, by way of imitation
observations.note: A vehement Imagination changes one's own body and sometimes another's; the word used is transmutation.

observations.quote: by a certaine kind of Vertue which the similitude of the Thing hath unto that Thing that is to be changed, which is moved by a vehement Imagination
observations.note: The means named: a virtue in the likeness between the thing and what is to be changed. Instances follow: swooning, teeth set on edge, yawning.

observations.quote: Many by their melancholly Imagination and diffidence have exposed themselves to the temptation of the uncleane Spirit
observations.note: A melancholy Imagination and distrust lay people open to the unclean Spirit, by which some have been overcome.

observations.quote: have so prevailed that on a sudden they have become the Temples of the living God
observations.note: The opposite case to MICRO.42: many by intent Imagination, firm Faith toward God, hope and prayer have suddenly become Temples of the living God.

observations.quote: True Faith is the cure of a false Imagination. Many fall sick and recover againe by the Faith of Imagination.
observations.note: True Faith is set against a false Imagination as its cure; sickness and recovery come by the Faith of Imagination.

observations.quote: The Sum of all is, that we worship God devoutly in honesty and holinesse
observations.note: The author gives the sum of the foregoing: to worship God devoutly in honesty and holiness.

observations.quote: as the more secret Theosophers or wise-hearted to God well know
observations.note: This is said to be well known to a few: the more secret Theosophers, Englished as wise-hearted to God.

observations.quote: the Understanding or Mind flaming with a Religious love, is joyned to the separated Intelligences
observations.note: By the devout intention of one who prays, the Understanding or Mind is joined to the separated Intelligences.

observations.quote: For internall Prayer proceeding with abundance of affection from a Godly mind, and continued with a fervent desire, uniteth the mind with God, and learneth and knoweth all things of God.
observations.note: Internal Prayer unites the mind with God and learns all things of God.

observations.quote: more few by far there are who know how to exercise the same by a supernaturall influence which doth rule and governe the body
observations.note: Few think what the Mind disposed by true faith can do, and far fewer know how to exercise it.

observations.quote: by reason of worldly cares and thoughtfulnesse wherewith they are overwhelmed, they can doe nothing that favoureth of true Wisdome
observations.note: Many know this disposition but, overwhelmed by worldly cares, can do nothing of true Wisdom.

observations.quote: Such like contemplations as these which are of greatest Antiquity will seem harsh and crabbed to the rude and vulgar sort of men; for few read them, and fewer understand them
observations.note: These contemplations, called of greatest Antiquity, are said to seem harsh to the vulgar and to be read by few and understood by fewer.

observations.quote: they require a larger narration then can be made of them at this time. To returne therefore to our purpose.
observations.note: With 'But thus much of these things' the author breaks off: the matter needs a fuller account than he gives now, and he returns to his purpose.

observations.quote: The purified Mind, like a river, entereth into the very inmost secrets of things, beyond all shadowes.
observations.note: The purified Mind enters the inmost secrets of things.

observations.quote: It is of greatest concernment that all Chymists should bewell acquaintedwith this true Fundamentall of the occult Phylosophycal Physick
observations.note: The author says all Chymists should know this, which he calls the true Fundamentall of the occult Phylosophycal Physick.

observations.quote: because of the Harmonicall concord and conspiration between the superiour and inferiour things of the greater and lesser world
observations.note: The reason given: the accord between the higher and lower things of the greater and the lesser world.

observations.quote: Petrus Severinus the Dane, together with Pratensis that faithfull Achates, deserveth to be numbred among the Ancient wise men
observations.note: The author ranks Petrus Severinus, with Pratensis, next to Paracelsus in clearing this foundation.

observations.quote: having got perpetuall praise by discovering to the Children of Art and Truth, this firme and unmovable Foundation with much solid and unshaken verity in his Idaea of Paracelsean Physick
observations.name: Petrus Severinus
observations.note: The foundation is credited to a named writing of Petrus Severinus, his Idaea of Paracelsean Physick, said to disclose it to the Children of Art and Truth. No words of his are given in these lines.

observations.quote: my honoured friend Joseph Quercetan Councellour and most worthy Physitian to the King of France
observations.note: The adversaries of Severinus are said to have been confuted by Joseph Quercetan, whom the author calls his honoured friend.

observations.quote: Th: Bovius an Italian of Verona, and Th: Muffet an Englishman, the best Hermetick Physitians of this age
observations.note: Two more are named with Quercetan as having answered the adversaries; the author calls them the best Hermetick Physitians of this age.
